answer: Both events are expiries observed only on the local side, and neither settles the remote state transition. In a lease, the holder renews before expiry and the coordinator may reassign after expiry, creating a new epoch: a renewal that receives no response may have been committed, or may have been lost while the lease expired and a successor was granted authority. The old holder's clock and local belief are not the authority, and a paused holder can resume later, so a missed renewal makes ownership uncertain, not failed, and must not be read as a successful renewal. A request timeout has the same shape: it is only a local wait bound, the server may have committed the effect before the reply was lost, and cancellation does not undo a committed effect, so no answer does not mean no commit. The workflow must preserve what is needed to resolve the ambiguity rather than guess: a stable logical operation identity (scoped to owner, payload and a declared retention window) that survives retries and leader changes; a durable authoritative outcome record - new, in-progress, committed, rejected or incompatible duplicate - committed atomically with the effect, retained for the retry/reconciliation horizon and queryable when an acknowledgment is lost; for ownership, a monotonic epoch/fencing token persisted and checked atomically at the destination, with a defined takeover linearization point and no token reuse; and the explicit unknown state itself, so it is reconciled or repaired and never collapsed into false success or false failure.
